findings.title: Staleness was scored as an outage -- in the freshness arm itself, not only in the value arm

two_prior_statements_of_this_finding_wer.in_0348_record: 'A perishable PASS is not marked perishable where it is read.' Vague, and it named no mechanism.
two_prior_statements_of_this_finding_wer.in_the_first_draft_of_this_record: 'The age bound EXISTS and is honest: analytics-is-fresh and otel-jsonl-is-fresh use world_or_blind, so staleness yields BLIND, not WORLD_FAIL.' FACTUALLY WRONG. I read the helper's NAME and assumed its semantics instead of reading its signature.
two_prior_statements_of_this_finding_wer.why_it_was_wrong: world_or_blind(name, field_present, value_ok) takes FIELD PRESENCE as its first argument. The arms were written world_or_blind(name, age >= 0, age <= MAX). A stale age IS present -- it is merely large -- so field_present was true, value_ok was false, and the arm scored a WORLD FAILURE. Staleness was reported as an outage by the very arm whose comment said 'BLIND, not PASS: the property was not observable at this candidate because nobody rendered it recently.'
two_prior_statements_of_this_finding_wer.lesson: Prose is not code, for the third time today, and this time in the file that documents that lesson most carefully. The comment stated the correct intent; the code did the opposite; nothing compared them.

findings.true_root_cause: Two distinct defects in the same oracle, both about staleness: (a) the freshness arms themselves scored stale as WORLD_FAIL (this is what produced the oscillation), and (b) the value arm analytics-declares-twelve-catalog-targets used world_count, which knows 'unreadable' but not 'stale', so it read a value out of a file whose age a DIFFERENT arm bounded. A guard in a different arm from the read it licenses gates nothing.
findings.third_arm_was_already_correct: otel-jsonl-has-one-line-per-span folded the freshness test INTO world_or_blind's field_present argument, so it blinded correctly. The author got it right in one arm of three. That is what made the defect hard to see from the comments alone.
findings.correction_to_0348: The 0348 record said 'a perishable PASS is not marked perishable where it is read.' That was imprecise. The age bound EXISTS and is honest: otel-jsonl-is-fresh and analytics-is-fresh use world_or_blind, so staleness yields BLIND, not WORLD_FAIL, and the header comment says so explicitly.
findings.actual_mechanism: formal/mojo/context_path_kpi_oracle.mojo:253 scores analytics-declares-twelve-catalog-targets with world_count, a HARD arm, on a value read from the same file whose freshness a DIFFERENT arm checks. world_count maps observed<0 to BLIND (unreadable) but has no notion of stale. So a 1600-minute-old file with a drifted value reports world:...:got-N-want-12 -- an outage -- while analytics-is-fresh independently reports BLIND. The freshness guard and the value read are in different arms.
findings.generalisation: Same shape as everything else in this session: an arm that READS a file is not an arm that VALIDATED that file.
findings.oscillation_observed: PASS yesterday -> WORLD_FAIL at ~04:00Z today (artifact age 1600 min, MAX_ARTIFACT_AGE_MIN 1440, crossing ~01:34Z) -> PASS again at 20:36Z today (age 31 min; the renderer ran at 20:05:00Z). No code changed on any side. The verdict tracks an external renderer's schedule.

fix.substrate: formal/mojo/oracle_substrate.mojo gains world_count_fresh(name, observed, expected, age_min, max_age_min) -- a four-way arm: unreadable => BLIND, age unknowable => BLIND, stale => BLIND, else compare. And world_fresh(name, age_min, max_age_min), which DELEGATES to it with observed=expected=0 rather than restating the logic. Zero-muda: one implementation of staleness in this substrate, not two that agree until they drift.

fix.call_sites: context_path_kpi_oracle.mojo: otel-jsonl-is-fresh and analytics-is-fresh now use world_fresh; analytics-declares-twelve-catalog-targets now uses world_count_fresh gated on an_age and MAX_ARTIFACT_AGE_MIN.

findings.title: The plane lock's retry bound was unguarded against a zero interval
findings.found_by: Local Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (Caste05, http://razr15-1.tail55d152.ts.net:8000), remote_tokens_billed = 0, 1166 total tokens, 8.3 s
findings.mechanism: tries = max 1 (int_of_float (timeout /. interval)) with no guard on interval. At interval = 0.0 that is int_of_float infinity -- undefined, in practice either zero polls or a hot spin.
findings.significance: A zero interval is exactly what formal/lean/UosBackgroundWaiterTwin.lean's `admissible` forbids (intervalMs = 0 => inadmissible). The file written to fix an unbounded busy-wait was itself violating the admissibility rule its sibling twin proves.
findings.fix: interval clamped to 0.05 when <= 0; tries clamped to 100000.
findings.control: A dedicated probe confirms that at interval = 0.0 acquire still terminates AND a forked child is still refused -- i.e. the clamp did not disable locking.
findings.tier_honesty: Three of Qwen's four findings did not survive checking: it claimed the retry loop lets two processes believe they hold the lock (control C2 empirically disproves this, and C2 is killed by a lockf-less mutant), and that the timeout path closes the fd without returning None (the code returns None). Advisory output, verified rather than trusted, per SC-INTEL-ROUTING-001 clause 6.

findings.title: The lock's acquire budget was shorter than its own longest legitimate hold, so writers aborted instead of waiting
findings.found_by: the F-W-19 re-sweep, which aborted rather than running
findings.observed: tools/mojo_mutation_dataplane.ml was wired `with_plane_lock "formal-mojo"` with NO explicit timeout and inherited the module default of 120.0. The other three call sites all passed ~timeout:600.0. The re-sweep therefore died with: 'uos_plane_lock: could not acquire /home/an/NAS-setup/uos/var/locks/formal-mojo.lock within 120s. Another writer or reader holds the plane. Nothing was mutated.'
findings.why_this_matters_more_than_a_tuning_nit: lean_mojo_differential.ml holds the plane for its ENTIRE 18-pair run, about two minutes. With a 120s writer budget, any mutation sweep started while a differential is running would abort. The lock would not be serialising access, it would be starving the writer -- the failure moved rather than being removed. It failed CLOSED, which is correct and safe, and that safety is exactly what made the defect easy to mistake for working-as-intended.
findings.the_invariant_now_stated_in_the_module: The acquire budget MUST be at least as long as the longest legitimate hold of the same plane.
findings.fix: Module default raised from 120.0 to 600.0 for both `acquire` and `with_plane_lock`, matching the three sites that already passed it; the mutation site also states 600.0 explicitly so the budget is visible where the tree is actually mutated. The failure mode of a caller that forgets is now 'waits longer', not 'aborts the run'. A caller that genuinely wants to fail fast passes a short timeout deliberately.
findings.verification: uos-plane-lock --selftest 5 controls, 0 failures, after the change; all four call sites grep as ~timeout:600.0.
findings.note_on_how_it_surfaced: I held the plane for 300s to make the F-W-19 edit and started the re-sweep 30 seconds later. The writer's 120s budget expired before my own hold did, so I starved my own sweep. The cause was mine; the defect it exposed was real and would have hit any differential/mutation overlap.

findings.title: A stale IN_FLIGHT journal wedged the mutation instrument for twelve hours, with an unfollowable recovery
findings.severity: operationally the most consequential finding in this record
findings.discovered: 2026-11-07T20:56Z, by a final-state hygiene sweep that used the CORRECT path
findings.mechanism: var/mutation/IN_FLIGHT.json, written 2026-11-07T08:35:54Z, named tools/uos-wait.ml with backup tools/uos-wait.ml.mutbak. The backup was absent. refuse_if_in_flight therefore refused EVERY invocation of tools/mojo_mutation_dataplane.ml -- the project's primary data-plane verification instrument -- from 08:35:54Z until it was fixed, roughly twelve hours, and nothing reported it.
findings.why_the_recovery_was_impossible: The refusal printed 'Restore the path it names from its .mutbak, delete both, and re-run.' That backup had already been deleted. A refusal whose instructions cannot be carried out is not fail-closed; it is wedged -- it stops the work without offering a way back.
findings.root_cause: with_mutation's restore path is ordered: write the original back, VERIFY byte-for-byte (fatal otherwise), remove the backup, remove the journal. Both removes were `try ... with _ -> ()`. The journal unlink failed silently after a restore that had already succeeded and been verified.
findings.sound_inference_the_fix_rests_on: Because the verify precedes the backup unlink, a MISSING backup proves the restore ran and was verified. So backup-absent is not evidence of a corrupt tree; it is evidence of a completed one. The tree was in fact sound: tools/uos-wait.ml --selftest reported '5 rules checked, 0 failed'.
fix: refuse_if_in_flight now discriminates: backup PRESENT => a real interrupted mutation, refuse and print the exact cp/rm command that recovers it, because the backup exists to be copied back; backup ABSENT => stale, say so and clear it.
The journal unlink in with_mutation now reports its failure. Not fatal -- the restore already succeeded and verified, so aborting would discard a good result -- but no longer silent.
findings.my_own_false_clean: At 20:35Z this session checked `governance/mutation/IN_FLIGHT.json` and reported 'absent'. That path does not exist; the journal lives at `var/mutation/IN_FLIGHT.json` (tools/mojo_mutation_dataplane.ml:173). An absence was read as health. Same defect class as F-W-07 (a scanner reporting 0 suspects after reading 0 bytes) and as the symlink-overlay failure: a check pointed at nothing cannot fail.
findings.scope_of_the_0348_record: That record's hygiene line was written at 04:17Z, before 08:35Z, and was true then. Its mirror sweep figures (116 mutants, 29 mirrors) predate the wedge and stand. No claim there is retracted.

findings.title: A crashing forked child in an OCaml toplevel script resumes the toplevel and re-emits the verdict
findings.found_by: the pid-file mutant of this session's own selftest
findings.mechanism: tools/uos-plane-lock.ml is run as an OCaml TOPLEVEL script. An uncaught exception in a forked child does not terminate the child; it returns control to the toplevel, which evaluates the REMAINING phrases -- including `let () = ... selftest ()`. findings.fix: The C5 child is wrapped so it never returns to the toplevel on any path, and exits via Unix._exit.

F-W-21.title: Ontology receipt arm scores staleness as WORLD_FAIL (CANDIDATE, WITHDRAWN)
F-W-21.why_i_thought_it_was: ontology_atlas_oracle.mojo:383 puts `receipt_fresh` (age <= MAX and pairs >= oracles_on_disk) in world_or_blind's VALUE slot, so a stale or partial receipt scores WORLD_FAIL. That is the F-W-14 shape, and the file's own comment eighteen lines above says 'Anything less is BLIND'.
F-W-21.why_it_is_not: `receipt_fresh` is this arm's SUBJECT, not its precondition. The arm is NAMED differential-receipt-is-fresh-and-complete; reporting a stale receipt is the whole job. I had already written the edit moving it into the presence slot when I saw that this makes value_ok true whenever field_present is true -- the arm could then never fail. I would have closed a WORLD_FAIL by making it unreportable, in the one arm whose purpose is catching stale evidence (INV-FALSIFY).
F-W-21.not_a_counterexample: agent_profile_oracle.mojo:303 tests the same expression in the PRESENCE slot, correctly, because it gates a different claim (obligation6-subject-actually-elaborates) on receipt quality. Same expression, different role. The two arms wiring it differently is correct, not a disagreement.

F-W-22.title: Lean/Mojo divergence in computeUtilityScore at latencyMs = 0
F-W-22.defect: FormalModelEvaluationSuite.lean:124 guarded lScore on `m.latencyMs < 2000` only; model_evaluation_suite_lib.mojo:72 guards on `latency_ms < 2000 and latency_ms > 0`. At latencyMs = 0 Lean awarded (2000-0)*25/20 = 2500 and Mojo awarded 0.
F-W-22.why_it_matters: latencyMs = 0 is not a hypothetical boundary -- it is the value every FAILED probe carries, because total_time_ms is only assigned when the response contains a timing field. The two implementations diverged precisely on the degenerate input, and the divergence paid out its largest single term (2500 of a nominal 1000-point scale) for a request that never completed. AK-47: it has to work on the degenerate input.
F-W-22.fix: Lean corrected to the Mojo semantics (`0 < m.latencyMs && m.latencyMs < 2000`), not the reverse: a zero round-trip was not measured, and an unmeasured latency is not an instantaneous one. No theorem referenced computeUtilityScore, so nothing was weakened to accommodate the change -- which is itself a finding: a scoring function with no law over it.

F-W-23.title: A probe budget shorter than the subject's failure latency reports a definite failure as unobservable
F-W-23.defect: razr15_max_qwen_oracle probed with `curl --max-time 12`; razr15-1:8000 returns a definite 502 after 120.1 s, because the gateway applies a 120 s timeout to its own backend (max_qwen_server.py:602). The probe could not be there when the answer arrived, read empty, and reported BLIND field-absent. model_evaluation_oracle, probing the SAME endpoint, parsed status 0 and scored it as three WORLD_FAILs. Two oracles, one endpoint, two verdicts from the same evidence; exactly one could be right and the difference was their patience, not the world.
F-W-23.mirror_of_f_w_14: F-W-14 scored unobservability as an outage (over-reporting). This scored an outage as unobservability (under-reporting). Same root pathology both times: the verdict was decided by the measuring apparatus instead of by the measurement.
F-W-23.second_defect_found_while_fixing_the_fir: The first fix was `curl --max-time 150` at the call site. It was INERT: oracle_substrate.capture wraps every probe in `timeout -k 5 PROBE_TIMEOUT_SECS` with PROBE_TIMEOUT_SECS = 20, and the smaller outer bound dominates. So no arm built on capture could EVER observe that 502, and a fix that looks right and changes nothing is worse than no fix because it stops the search. Caught by running it rather than by reading it.
F-W-23.fix: (1) New shared Receipt.world_status(name, http_code, body_ok): no status / 000 / 0 -> BLIND; status present and != 200 -> WORLD_FAIL; 200 -> body decides. Both oracles now share one implementation of what an HTTP probe result means, so they cannot disagree about one endpoint again. (2) capture() gains an optional per-call bound; 20 s stays the default (it is the guard that stops an oracle inheriting its subject's hang) and a caller needing longer must say so and say why at the call site. (3) Both call sites set 150 s > the gateway's own 120 s. A long budget costs nothing on a healthy endpoint and costs time only when something is actually wrong, which is when the definite answer is worth waiting for.
F-W-23.verified: razr15_max_qwen_oracle went from BLIND(2) 'field-absent' to WORLD_FAIL 'gateway-completes-a-bounded-chat:http-502' -- severity ROSE, the outage is named, blind 2 -> 0, world_checks 21 -> 22.

F-W-27.title: razr15-1:8000 returns HTTP 200 with a zero-byte body for chat completions
F-W-27.status: OBSERVED LIVE -- gateway-side, not fixed here
F-W-27.evidence: Direct curl, independent of any oracle parsing: `HTTP=200 bytes=0 time=0.368490` at 20261108-0032Z, same host/model/payload that returned a 502 after 120.1s at 2259Z and a correct completion at 2325Z. The gateway is flapping between three distinct failure modes.

F-W-27.correction_to_prior_record: The prior record localised F-W-27 to the :8000 gateway while :8081 answered correctly, which was right, and implied a standing fault, which was wrong. At 20261108-0702Z the gateway answered 10/10 probes with a valid 5316-5323 byte completion. The fault is NOT currently reproducing in the wild. I did not conclude from that it was fixed, which would have repeated the razr15-was-down error in the opposite direction.
root_cause_located_structurally: Non-streaming path: the enrichment block is wrapped in `except Exception: pass`, correct for telemetry, but it meant an EMPTY or NON-JSON backend body fell through to send_response(resp.status) and was relayed to the client as 200 with Content-Length: 0.

Streaming path: send_response and end_headers were called BEFORE reading any byte of the backend stream. A stream that opened and closed produced 200 with 0 bytes, and because the status line was already committed the `except` handler could no longer send its 502. The status was decided before the evidence for it existed.

Both are the third HTTP failure mode named in the F-W-23 analysis -- 200 with a bad or empty body -- the one a `status == 200` check reports as a FALSE PASS. F-W-23 fixed the oracle side; this fixes the producer side, so the mode stops being produced.
F-W-27.timing_evidence: The observed failures were 0.07-0.37 s, far too fast for the 180 s backend timeout, i.e. a stream or body that terminated immediately rather than one that hung.
fix: Streaming: first line hoisted above the headers; an empty stream becomes 502 with uos_finding F-W-27.

Non-streaming: explicit validation separate from enrichment -- empty body => 502, non-JSON => 502, and on the chat path only, JSON without `choices` => 502. The choices requirement is gated on the chat path because /v1/embeddings answers with `data` and demanding choices everywhere would 502 a healthy surface.

`except Exception: pass` => a recorded reason surfaced as X-UOS-Enrichment-Failed. The caller's verdict is unchanged; only the silence is removed. An unexplained absence of telemetry is indistinguishable from telemetry never configured.

I double-backgrounded the differential (nohup & inside a run_in_background Bash call), so the wrapper exited immediately while the real process detached, and the completion notification reported the wrapper rather than the run.

Fixed by serving a canned response from a file written with printf.
